major.name: Anthropology - BA

items.label: One Methods Course
items.notes: ANTH 129 and ANTH 182 apply to the 40 upper-division units required.

requirement.label: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
requirement.description: All upper-division ANTH classes are eligible, including Senior Thesis Sequence (ANTH 195A, 195B, 195C). See General Catalog.
requirement.notes: Courses from the Related Fields List (on the Anthropology Department website) and other related courses deemed appropriate by the Anthropology Department may be applied to this area by petition only, but a minimum of 28 units towards the upper division major must be satisfied by Anthropology courses. Anthropology Majors must meet all prerequisites and restrictions set by the home department of the Related Fields List course in order to enroll in the course. Students are encouraged to discuss Related Fields List course selections with an Anthropology Undergraduate Advisor.

narrative:
MAJOR REGULATIONS
PREREQUISITES Check the General Catalog for the prerequisites to all listed courses.
P/NP GRADING OPTION Up to 4 units of the following courses may be taken P/NP for major credit: Anthropology 178, 183, 190. All other courses (Prep and UD) must be completed on a letter-grade basis.
SUBSTITUTIONS In the major requirements permissible only by petition to the department chair and dean.
G.P.A REQUIREMENTS At least 2.0 overall UC average in all upper-division major courses and all courses (Prep and UD) for the major.
DOUBLE MAJORS With the approval of each department chairperson, up to a total of 8 units may be applied simultaneously to both UD majors

nodes.title: Introductory Cultural Anthropology
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower Division Anthropology
nodes.description: The nature of culture: survey of the range of cultural phenomena, including material culture, social organization, religion, and other topics.

nodes.title: World Archaeology
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower Division Anthropology
nodes.description: An introduction to archaeology and the history of humankind from the earliest times through the advent of literate civilization and cities, also processes of cultural change and the importance of archaeology to people and societies today. Partly self-paced learning.

nodes.title: Introduction to Archaeology
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower Division Anthropology
nodes.description: Introduction to archaeology and the prehistory of humankind from the earliest times up to the advent of civilization and cities, also processes of cultural change.

nodes.title: Introductory Biological Anthropology
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower Division Anthropology
nodes.description: An introductory course in human evolutionary biology. Natural selection and its genetic basis are used to highlight a variety of human traits. The fossil record is addressed, but the course takes more of an adaptationist than a paleontological perspective.

nodes.title: Introductory Biosocial Anthropology
nodes.description: An introduction to our evolved, universal human nature, the evolution of the human mind, and how they shape behavior, social life, and culture. Topics include friendship, mate choice, incest avoidance, cooperation, revenge, status, jealousy, emotions, group formation, and intergroup aggression.

nodes.title: Methods in the Human Behavioral Sciences
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: One Methods Course
nodes.description: Introduces the design and analysis of scientific studies on human behavior. Emphasizes theory-based testing of hypotheses, with examples drawn from human ecology, physiology, and behavior. Covers a range of quantitative and qualitative methods including observation, surveys, and experiments.

nodes.title: Basic Archaeological Concepts
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: A survey of important archaeological methods of excavation, analysis, and interpretation. Focus will be on the problems and promise of various approaches to the explanation of past human behavior.

nodes.title: Activist Anthropology
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Activist scholarship seeks to combine rigorous research and political commitment to achieve empirical and theoretical understanding of social processes. While open access to information has democratized knowledge production, academic work is still necessary to ask the questions and find the answers to address social injustice and inequality. In this course, we explore the methods and results of more than two decades of activist research.

nodes.title: Human-Wildlife Interactions
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Survey of human-wildlife interactions (e.g., bushmeat, pet trade, crop-raiding). Students examine cascading effects on wildlife, landscapes, and human populations, as well as mitigating approaches relating to our changing perceptions of wildlife and nature.

nodes.title: Biology of Women
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: An exploration of female and womxn’s reproductive lives from an evolutionary and biocultural perspective. We will focus on physiological, ecological, and social aspects of womxn’s development across cultures from before birth, through reproductive processes like pregnancy, birth, lactation, menopause, and aging. Examples will be drawn from contemporary human societies, including many small-scale societies, although non-human primates will also be considered occasionally. This class will include lectures, discussion in multiple formats, and other modes of learning.

nodes.title: Cultural Evolution
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.prereq_text: Upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: This course takes a scientific and evolutionary lens to cultural phenomena. We will consider the origins of culture in non- humans and humans, and how tendencies to imitate, conform, teach and uphold social norms via punishment and reward shape behavioral variation.

nodes.title: Educating the Native
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: We look at different educational projects, such as Indian boarding Schools, English-only laws, the "indirect rule" of the British colonies. We address the not-always-clear line between education as a form of social control or as a form of liberation.

nodes.title: Human Universals
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: A critical overview of those characteristics of human psyche, behavior, society, and culture that are allegedly found among all peoples: the constants of human nature.

nodes.title: The Anthropology of Food
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Critical survey of different anthropological approaches to food production and consumption. Topics may include relations between agricultural forms and political systems; the meanings of feasting; cooking; class, race, and gender; food and national identity; food sovereignty, food justice and more.

nodes.title: Indigenous People and the Nation State in the Americas
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: The changing relationship between indigenous people and the state. Compare the differences and similarities between indigenous peoples' mobilizations in the cases of Canada, USA, Ecuador, Chile, Guatemala, Bolivia and Mexico.

nodes.title: Structuralism and Structural Functionalism
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Outlines a segment of the history of anthropological theory through the 20th century ethnological traditions of structuralism and structural functionalism. Foregrounds select anthropologists who have contributed to these traditions, including Emile Durkheim, E.E. Evans-Pritchard and Eduardo Viveros de Castro; their critics: Judith Butler, Saba Mahmood, and Marilyn Strathern. The goal of the course is to organize the discursive structure around which these thinkers cohere and to question the place of these traditions in contemporary anthropology. Topics of interest include institutions/agency; nature/culture; subsistence, desire, and need; language and semiotics; magic/religion; gender/sexuality; and ontology/metaphysics.

nodes.title: Language, Culture, and Place
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Focuses on the dialectical interplay between humans and the environment and how people use language to classify, make sense of, and attribute moral and symbolic meaning to places and landscapes.

nodes.title: Myth, Ritual and Symbol
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Uses ethnographic case studies, films and performance videos to explore myth, ritual, and symbolism cross-culturally. Compares and contrasts the symbolic dimensions of gender and ethnic identity, world view, social and political organization and change in different societies.

nodes.title: Borders and Borderlands
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: The theoretical concept of "borderlands" examined through a discussion of the societies, economics and cultures that form on geopolitical borders. The Mexico-U.S. border will be discussed in detail.

nodes.title: Psychological and Phenomenological Anthropology
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Examines a subfield of anthropology whose conceptual frameworks rely on traditions of phenomenology, psychoanalysis, and psychology. The course focuses on the emergence of this subfield, its texts and discourses, and its importance for anthropological inquiry. It also explores the themes it foregrounds, including medicine, the body, the imagination, existence, therapeutic worlds, addiction, gender and sexuality, religious traditions, shamanism, and colonialism. Throughout our readings we also consider the deep affinities between anthropology, phenomenology, and psychoanalysis, how they have historically intersected, and their relevance for contemporary anthropological analysis.

nodes.title: Genetics, Natural Selection, and Human Evolution
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: An introduction to the nature and role of genes in evolution, in natural selection, in sexual reproduction, in cellular regulation, in human development, in structuring universal human adaptive design, and in creating individual and intergroup similarities and differences.

nodes.title: Anthropology of Security
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Examines the infrastructures, practices, and concepts that emerge from securitization. Critically analyzes how security becomes entangled with the state as a legal, political, and social form and how securitization marks a new mode of power and governance irreducible to the demands of sovereignty. Topics include the relationship between freedom, rights, and protection; surveillance and its technologies; material and immaterial violence; global networks and the international; force and coercion; policing and law enforcement; and the politics of borderlands and migration.

nodes.title: Feeding Ecology of Primates and Humans
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Foraging and feeding patterns in primates with some discussion of human patterns. Topics include digestive physiology; measurement of energy flows and food availability; foraging theory; and the evolutionary context of human diets.

nodes.title: Data Analysis for the Social Sciences with R
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: An introduction to the scientific process and data analysis using the programming language R. Students harness fundamentals of data manipulation, visualization, and research workflows to refine and present hypotheses and results on social science datasets. Introduces modeling methods.

nodes.title: Capitalism
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: This course presents the contribution of Marxist analysis to anthropology. Among the topics explored are: the commodity; accumulation; reproduction; class; peasants and capital; land and labor; hegemony.

nodes.title: Anthropology of Gender
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: The cross-cultural study of gender from a feminist perspective. Topics may include gender, race, and class; gender and nature; gender and the division of labor; gender and kinship; gender and subjectivity; gender and sexuality; gender and the state; gender and knowledge/discourse.

nodes.title: Laboratory Methods and Biomarkers for the Social Sciences
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: This course spans a broad range of theory and methods involved in using biomarkers in the social sciences. Theory comes from areas of behavioral research including, behavioral endocrinology, behavioral ecology, evolutionary medicine, and public health. Methods focus on but are not limited to biomarker sampling (saliva, urine, feces, blood), quality controls and processing, and the principles of immunoassays used to measure biomarker concentrations.

nodes.title: Anthropology of Racial Slavery
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Examines the world-building and world-destroying structures produced from the transatlantic slave trade. While the primary focus is the formation of slavery in the United States, readings will also consider the place of Africa and Latin America in relation to the transatlantic slave trade. Fundamentally, the course introduces students to the numerous mechanisms used to maintain the being of the slave as slave through the law, political economy, criminal justice, and in the organization of political and social life. We will pay attention to the encounters slavery made possible between intersecting worlds and the concepts that underly this relationship between worlds: including debt, freedom, race, rights, the human, and value.

nodes.title: Ethnographic Research Methods: Ethics and Engagement
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: One Methods Course
UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Interrogation of ethnographic research, its development and its ethical implications. Weighing approaches such as participatory action research, engaged and collaborative research, and decolonized methodologies. Students will develop projects based on a critical reading of these models.

nodes.title: Behavioral Ecology of Hunter Gatherers
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: A thorough introduction using a behavioral ecology approach to the diversity of behaviors found among foragers in Africa, South America, Southeast Asia, and Australia. Topics include: diet and subsistence, mating, demography, social behavior, mobility and settlement patterns, gender, indigenous rights, and conservation.

nodes.title: International Development and Population Health
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Considers the distribution and determinants of well being in human populations, with an emphasis on low-income nations and the actions of the international development sector. Focus is placed on cultural/social determinants of health, including issues of gender equality. Takes a critical perspective on the tools used to measure population health and the design and evaluation of development policy and interventions.

nodes.title: Anthropology of Law
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Examines the way the law and legal apparatuses binds subjects (human and otherwise) to the material world. It does so by conceptually analyzing what the law is and the experiences it creates as they are depicted in legal discourse, the historical archive, and ethnography. Topics include rights, freedoms, and entitlements; crime and punishment; slavery and servitude; the formation of constitutional power; status laws and the logic of race that undergirds them; and the subterranean political, social, and economic desires that the law seeks to exploit and animate within “the people.”

nodes.title: Cultural Development in Mesoamerica
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: The rise and fall of various ancient civilizations such as those of the Maya, Aztecs, Toltecs, Teotihuacanos, and Olmec as well as their cultural antecedents. This course uses self-paced audiovisual modules as well as traditional lecture format.

nodes.title: Cultural Anthropology of Latin America
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Contemporary issues of rural and urban societies in the Caribbean, and Central and South America. Examination of continuities and changes in cultural institutions and values; inequality, colonialism, settler colonialism, state formation, indigenous social movements, race, gender, class and ethnicity, urbanization, extractivism.

nodes.title: Interdisciplinary Approaches to the History and Societies of Latin America and Iberia
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Issues central to the study of Latin America and Iberia across the social sciences and history. Topics include nationalism, revolution, politics and the state, economic development and international relations, labor, popular culture, race, gender, religion, migration, environment, imperialism, and colonialism.

nodes.title: Cultural Anthropology of Mexico
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: An examination of contemporary issues in Mexico through an anthropological lens. Topics may include race, class, gender, and sexuality, nation-state formation, settler colonialism, decolonization, social movements, and political economy.

nodes.title: Language and Social Signs
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Explores a tradition of anthropological inquiry that builds an account of language as a system of socially intelligible signs. Often referred to as semiotics, this class examines how signs and language become the conduits for thinking about and understanding our relationship with the world, our shared social and political ecologies, and how our interpretation of such signs is expressive of larger structures that lie inside of us. Topics and concepts for exploration include the relationship between language, signs, and symbols; structuralism and poststructuralism; performativity and performance; practice and action; ontology and metaphysics; discourse and discursive agency; and speech and communicative rationality.

nodes.title: The Ancient Maya
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: The splendiferous Maya civilization as it waxed and waned during ancient times.

nodes.title: Anthropology of Environmental Health
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.prereq_text: ANTH 2 or equivalent introduction to sociocultural anthropology
nodes.description: A sociocultural medical anthropological approach to explore how environmental hazards, many of them human-influenced, shape health and illness around the world. Topics include environmental risk and perception, industrial toxics, disasters, environmental justice, and chronic disease.

nodes.title: Land of the Pharaohs: An Archaeology of Ancient Egypt
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Selected topics on the archaeology of ancient Egypt, placing the monuments of this great civilization in the context of its rise and development. Emphasis on ancient Egyptian material culture as a source for understanding Egyptian political, social, and economic dynamics.

nodes.title: Landback, Reparations, and Solidarity Economies
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: An introduction to two related topics that have become increasingly central in the US and beyond in recent years: rising demands for, and concrete steps toward, the return of lands to present day descendants of Native and Indigenous peoples who previously occupied these lands [colloquially known as "land back"]; and the payment of reparations [either monetary or in kind] to descendants of enslaved peoples, as partial compensation for the trauma, social suffering and economic loss of enslavement. We critically examine the arguments put forth to justify both flows of thought and action; we study actual cases where these actions have been taken; and we ask what can be learned.

nodes.title: Ethics in Archaeology
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: An analysis of ethics in contemporary archaeology. Topics include reburial and repatriation, interpretation of the archaeological record in the context of historically oppressed groups, ethnic minorities, and non-western societies. The course also includes the ethics of collecting and managing cultural property.

nodes.title: Anthropological Demography and Life History
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.prereq_text: Anthropology 5 or 7 or upper-division standing; or Environmental Studies 2 or 3.
nodes.description: Introduces students to anthropologic applications of demography and life history theory. Focuses on ecological approaches to population dynamics, birth and death processes, and policy implications in light of population "problems" among traditional and modern societies.

nodes.title: Water and Society
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Covers the longstanding debate over the relation between irrigation and state formation, as well as current developments in the study of water and society. Emphasis is placed on people living in arid and semi-arid environments.

nodes.title: Human Genetics
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.prereq_text: ANTH 5 or ANTH 7, ANTH 9 or equivalent.
nodes.description: Introduction to basic principles of genetics and genomics in human evolution. Topics covered include molecular evolution, population genetics, comparative genomics, epigenetics, gene-culture interactions and relevant social and ethical issues.

nodes.title: Evolutionary Psychology
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Surveys evolutionary psychology, examining traditional psychological topics through Darwinian lenses. Traditional psychology answers mechanistic questions about how perception, emotion, cognition, development and social interactions work. Evolutionary psychology addresses the complementary functional question of why they work the way they do.

nodes.title: Environmental Anthropology
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Examines the ways that humans interact with, use, and perceive the environment and nature, with a focus on the cultural, political, and economic features of human environment relationships across time and in different parts of the world. Through readings, in-class activities and discussions, field trips, and research projects, students will gain a better understanding of how anthropological theory, research, and applications can be used to address contemporary environment topics and problems.

nodes.title: Primate Behavior
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.prereq_text: Anthropology 5 or 7; not open to freshmen.
nodes.description: An introduction to primatology and the principles of behavioral ecology using langur, vervet, macaque, baboon, gorilla, and chimpanzee field studies to illustrate theories of foraging, parenting, kinship, sexual selection, incest avoidance, aggression, and dominance. Concludes with applications to human evolution.

nodes.title: The Anthropology of Africa
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: This course offers an overview of the anthropological studies of people on the African continent. Drawing from case studies in archaeology, historical linguistics, ethnography, biological anthropology and medical anthropology, this course documents a sea change from Africa under the gaze of the West, to Africa as examined and defined by African peoples from their own diverse and varied perspectives.

nodes.title: Ethnographic Field Methods
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Introduction to skills and tools of data collection through fieldwork in cultural anthropology. Emphasis on techniques, methods, and concepts of ethnographic research and how basic observational information is systematized for presentation, analysis, and cross-cultural comparison.

nodes.title: Anthropology of War
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Examines the concepts and experiences that cohere around warfare and weaponized conflict. Investigates the modern shape of war, its technologies, its strategies and how it’s infused within broader political and social life. Topics and concepts include military, civil, political, and social violence; insurgency and counterinsurgency; revolution and counterrevolution; enmity and the logics of race; power and force; sovereignty and territorial space; security and protection; and communicative reason and the lack thereof.

nodes.title: Prehistoric Food Production
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: A history of the process of plant and animal domestication in the Americas, the Near East, Asia, and Africa. Course focuses on the specific biological changes in the major domesticates as well as associated social changes in human life.

nodes.title: The Origins of Complex Societies
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Why and how complex societies developed from simple, egalitarian societies in some areas of the world. Course surveys major theories and evidence surrounding the origins of states and urban societies in New and Old World.

nodes.title: People of the Ice Age
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Human adaptations and population dispersals during the Ice Age (Pleistocene epoch). Course focuses on Stone Age cultures and the evidence for early human occupation of the Americas and the Old World between three million and 10,000 years ago.

nodes.title: Evolution of Cooperation
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Interdisciplinary focus on the emergence and maintenance of cooperation in human populations. Are we unique in our abilities to reap gains from cooperative endeavors? Why are some people generous, others stingy? How do propensities, personalities, ecology, and cultural institutions affect success in cooperation?

nodes.title: The Evolutionary Anthropology of Family Life
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Explores how evolutionary anthropologists study cultural diversity in human family life. Together we examine global variation in marriage systems, kinship and inheritance rules, parental investment, norms of sex and reproduction, and the role of extended kin. Each week pairs human examples with insights from non-human animals to ask what evolutionary theory reveals about the determinants of family structure, adaptation to local environments, and patterns of conflict and cooperation among family members.

nodes.title: Evolutionary Medicine
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.prereq_text: Anth 5 with a minimum grade of C; or, EEMB 2 and EEMB 3; or, MCDB 1 and MCDB 2.
nodes.description: Applies evolutionary principles to understanding human health and disease past and present. Topics include host/parasite co-evolution, aging and senescence, influence of human migration and culture on disease patterns, and evolutionary origins of diseases of civilization."

nodes.title: Amazonia
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Focuses on the people, environment, and history of Amazon basin. Topics of study include human-environment interactions across time; social and cultural groups; representations in film, media, and literature; and contemporary social, political, and environmental issues facing the region.

nodes.title: Medical Anthropology
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: This sociocultural anthropology course is focused on the social construction of health, risk, illness, and disease in the US and around the globe and research methods used to study them. Topics include health inequality and its social production, critical analysis of biomedicine and power, technologies of diagnosis and treatment, stigma and disability, gender, bodies and health, mental health and illness, medicalization and pharmaceuticalization, and global health and humanitarian care.

nodes.title: Temples, Tombs and Hieroglyphs: Ancient Egyptian Religion
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Examination of Ancient Egyptian religion from massive temples and pyramids to modest offerings and simple burials. The interaction of sacred and secular is considered through examination of the individual, society, and the state in shaping religious beliefs.

nodes.title: Human Reproduction Ecology and Endocrinology
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Regulation of reproductive function by diet, energy balance, lactation, and social context. The role of hormones in the regulation of human reproduction, behavior, and physiology. Hormonal changes with parenting and pregnancy in men and women.

nodes.title: Internship in Archaeological Record-Keeping and Collections
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Interns serve as assistants in the department's Central Coast Information Center or Repository for Archaeological Collections or both.

nodes.title: Archaeology of Ethnicity & Race
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Concepts of ethnicity and race are catalyzing forces today. Exploring the changing definitions and resonances of these categories in an archaeological context, we examine how these concepts shifted in antiquity and modern scholarship, with particular reference to Egypt, Nubia, and the Mediterranean.

nodes.title: Osteology
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Designed to teach students in archaeology and physical anthropology the basic skills necessary to identify and analyze the remains of animals recovered from archaeological excavations. Emphasis is placed on laboratory work with actual archaeological collections and testing hypotheses about prehistoric human behavior.

groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: One Methods Course

nodes.title: Introduction to Lithic Analysis
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: This course gives students an introduction to the anthropology and archaeology of making and using stone tools. Practical experience in making tools and using them experimentally is emphasized.

nodes.title: Internship in Archaeological Resource Management
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Interns serve as assistants or trainees in the archaeological programs of a governmental agency, a museum, or a private firm in the local area. In collaboration with the instructor and an extramural archaeologist, the student conceives a set of activities for the internship.

nodes.title: Lab Course in Paleoethnobotany
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Study of archaeological plant remains, including field/lab methodology, the reconstruction of ancient environment and the subsistence, spatial and temporal analysis, quantitative methods, and taxonomy. Divided between lecture, discussion, and labwork, involving microscopic identification of paleoethnobotanical remains.

nodes.title: Lab Course in Zooarchaeology
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Study of archaeological faunal remains, including field/lab methodology, the reconstruction of ancient environment and the subsistence, spatial and temporal analysis, quantitative methods, and taxonomy. Divided between lecture, discussion, and labwork, involving identification of zooarchaeological remains.

nodes.title: Problems in European Prehistory
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Seminar in selected problems in the archaeology of Europe.

nodes.title: Cultural Anthropology Internship
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Students serve as interns in various settings such as museums, governmental agencies, and health organizations to gain exposure to different cultures. In collaboration with the instructor and an extramural anthropologist, the student conceives a set of activities for the internship.

nodes.title: After graduation: Preparing for Graduate School and the Job Market
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.prereq_text: Juniors and Seniors only; limited to Anthropology Majors/Minors
nodes.description: This course is designed to guide students: (1) through the graduate school application process, and (2) in how to prepare for the job market. We will consider all steps and components of applying to graduate school. The second half of class will focus on best practices for finding jobs after graduation.

nodes.title: Field Training Archaeology
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Introduction to design of research projects and techniques of data collection in archaeology. The number of units taken in one course will depend on the amount of training and experience received.

nodes.title: Practicum in Field and Laboratory Analysis
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: An applied course emphasizing acquisition of practical skills in archaeological field work and laboratory analysis. Projects will vary depending on the type of archaeological research in progress and may include artifact processing, cataloguing, field excavation and preparation of research results.

nodes.title: Anthropology Honors Program: Research Design
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.prereq_text: Admission to Anthropology honors program; consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Formal classroom seminar to prepare students for the ANTH 195B and 195C Anthropology honors thesis sequence. This course guides students in formulating a research problem that they will pursue in ANTH 195B and 195C, including planning a research agenda and conducting background research that will frame their honors thesis project. Project completion will be carried out individually during ANTH 195B and 195C.

nodes.title: Biology of Women
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: An exploration of female and womxn’s reproductive lives from an evolutionary and biocultural perspective. We will focus on physiological, ecological, and social aspects of womxn’s development across cultures from before birth, through reproductive processes like pregnancy, birth, lactation, menopause, and aging. Examples will be drawn from contemporary human societies, including many small-scale societies, although non-human primates will also be considered occasionally. This class will include lectures, discussion in multiple formats, and other modes of learning. Recommended Prep: ANTH 5 or Equivalent ANTH Majors: Take for Letter Grade to apply for Major Requirements

nodes.title: Caring for Transformation: The Affect of Social Justice
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: This course recognizes the emotional effects of oppression. Recently, more attention shows how systemic mistreatment of people affects the social and economic wellbeing of communities (both systematically targeted by racism and colonization and those enforcing these systems). We will practice, reflect, discuss, and explore what healing from oppression looks like. We explore the emotional dimensions of oppression and justice while being aware that the history of injustice is full of intense emotions. How do we connect the personal, academic, and political experience of living and researching through these experiences? How do we analyze and heal the effects of injustice and mistreatment and support our academic practice and activist work?

nodes.title: Sensory Ecologies
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: This seminar critically examines how sensory experiences mediate various kinds of relationships, including between humans, nonhumans, and environments. Drawing from anthropology, science and technology studies (STS), environmental humanities, art theory and practice, and sensory ethnography, the course explores how ecologies are lived, perceived, created, and contested through embodied practice. We will analyze how sensory regimes are shaped by power hierarchies, labor, infrastructures, and histories, and how they inform knowledge production, governance, resistance, refusal, and creative endeavors. Students will engage multimodal methods to investigate how ecological relations, broadly conceived, are felt, negotiated, and made meaningful.

nodes.title: Field Methods in Biocultural Anthropology
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Research design and data collection are skills that are necessary for all researchers to propose and conduct successful research projects. The primary aims of this course are (1) to familiarize students with the process of designing a research project, (2) to introduce students to a variety of data collection methods typically used by cultural and biological anthropologists, as well as other social scientists, and (3) to provide students with hands-on experience and thorough feedback on designing and conducting their own projects.

nodes.title: Pathways of Indigenous Laws in Mexico
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: In this seminar, students take part in the research design of a survey research project in collaboration with an Organization of Indigenous Lawyers in Oaxaca. We analyze the interviews and fieldnotes of research conducted during June 2025 in Oaxaca, with indigenous authorities and other state authorities. In the class, students learn about the legal system in Mexico, Indigenous Customary Law, the discrimination faced by indigenous people in the legal system, and conflict resolution. Along with text analysis, coding and survey design.

nodes.title: The Science of Friendship
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: Ten courses from full Anthropology curriculum or a related field
nodes.description: Why are friendships so central to our daily lives? This class explores the causes and consequences of this fundamental human bond, traversing its roots in animal behavior, its underlying biology and psychology, its relationship with health, and both its diversity and universal features across human cultures.

nodes.title: Introduction to Environmental Studies
nodes.description: Environmental Studies requires insights from many disciplines, including the social as well as biophysical science and the humanities. This introduction offers an overview of the field, examining both our planet and the ways in which we humans depend on it.

nodes.title: Introduction to Environmental Science
nodes.description: Provides integration of fundamental science with environmental topics. Includes impacts of human population increase; principles of systems and change, biogeochemical cycles, ecosystems and global climate; energy and laws of thermodynamics; water supply and pollution; toxicology and risk analysis; air pollution and stratospheric ozone depletion.

nodes.title: Introduction to the Social and Cultural Environment
nodes.description: An introduction to the relationship of societies and the environment from prehistorical times to the present. The course is global in perspective, and includes history, literature, philosophy, economics, science, and culture as evidence for examining the human social environment.
